transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: An international team of astronomers has discovered a new Earth-sized planet orbiting a nearby star. The planet, named Proxima d, is located just 4.2 light-years away from our solar system, making it one of the closest exoplanets ever found. Scientists say the planet orbits within the star's habitable zone, where conditions might be suitable for liquid water to exist. The discovery was made using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope in Chile. Researchers note that while the planet's size is similar to Earth, its mass is only about a quarter of our planet's, suggesting it might be a rocky world with a thinner atmosphere. Follow-up studies are planned to determine the planet's atmospheric composition and whether it shows signs of potential life.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Female)
paras: The ancient city of Pompeii has unveiled another remarkable archaeological find: a perfectly preserved food stall, known as a thermopolium. The stall served hot food and drinks to Roman citizens nearly 2,000 years ago. Archaeologists found colorful frescoes depicting animals that were part of the menu, including ducks, roosters, and fish. They also discovered traces of pork, fish, snails, and beef in the terra-cotta jars used to store food. The thermopolium also contained a decorated bronze drinking bowl and wine flasks. Experts say this discovery provides extraordinary insight into daily life in Pompeii before the catastrophic eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD. The site will be opened to the public starting next month.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: A new zero-waste grocery store chain is expanding across Canada, with plans to open 20 new locations this year. The stores, called "Nada," allow customers to bring their own containers and purchase exactly the amount of food they need, eliminating packaging waste. Products range from grains and nuts to cleaning supplies and personal care items, all sold without plastic packaging. Since opening its first store in Vancouver in 2016, Nada has helped customers avoid over 2 million pieces of single-use plastic. The company reports that its customers reduce their household waste by an average of 75% after switching to zero-waste shopping. The expansion is being funded through a combination of private investment and community crowdfunding.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (David): Hi Emma, have you decided which elective courses you're taking next semester?
Woman (Emma): I'm still looking, David. I'm thinking about either photography or creative writing. What about you?
Man: I'm considering the astronomy course. I've always been fascinated by stars and planets. But I heard the professor is really tough.
Woman: Oh, Professor Henderson? Yeah, I've heard his exams are difficult, but people say his classes are fascinating. He brings a telescope to some evening sessions.
Man: That does sound amazing. I'm also looking at the digital marketing course, which might be more practical for my business degree.

Woman: That's a good point. You're a business major, right? The marketing course could help with your career. Photography is just for fun for me, but I might need it someday too since I'm a journalism major.
Man: Journalism and photography do go hand in hand. When do we need to register by the way?
Woman: Registration opens next Monday. But seniors get to register first, so we juniors have to wait until Wednesday.
Man: Oh right! I forgot about that. Do you want to meet up before then to look at the course catalog together?
Woman: Sure! How about tomorrow afternoon in the library? We can compare schedules and make sure we don't have time conflicts.
Man: Perfect. I'll see you then at 2 PM.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man: Good afternoon, ma'am. How can I assist you at the post office today?
Woman: Hi, I need to send this package to my sister in Chicago. What's the fastest way to get it there?
Man: Priority Mail Express would get it there overnight by 10:30 AM tomorrow, but it's pretty expensive. Priority Mail would take two days and cost less.
Woman: It's her birthday present, so I'd like it to get there quickly. But overnight is really pricey. What about regular Priority Mail?
Man: That would be delivered by Wednesday, guaranteed. If we send it today, that's two business days. Let me weigh your package first. It's 2 pounds, 4 ounces.
Woman: How much would that be?
Man: Priority Mail to Chicago would be $13.75. Express would be $38.95.
Woman: Priority is fine, then. Can I get tracking with that?
Man: Yes, tracking is included automatically. Would you like to add insurance? The package looks valuable.
Woman: It's a necklace, so probably worth about $150. How much is insurance?
Man: Insurance up to $200 would be an extra $3.50.
Woman: Yes, let's add that. Can I also get delivery confirmation so I know when she receives it?
Man: That's already included with tracking. You'll get an email notification when it's delivered. Just fill out this form with your sister's address.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Female)
paras: The British tradition of afternoon tea dates back to the 1840s, when Anna, the seventh Duchess of Bedford, started asking for tea, bread, butter, and cakes around four o'clock in the afternoon. At that time, dinner was served fashionably late at eight o'clock, leaving a long period between lunch and dinner. The Duchess found this gap difficult and began inviting friends to join her for this afternoon meal. The tradition quickly spread among upper-class society and eventually became a formal social occasion. Traditional afternoon tea includes a selection of finger sandwiches, scones with clotted cream and jam, and a variety of sweet pastries and cakes. Tea, of course, is the central element, typically served in fine bone china cups. Today, afternoon tea is enjoyed in hotels, tea rooms, and homes across Britain and has become popular around the world as a symbol of British culture and hospitality.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Male)
paras: Scientists have been studying the effects of blue light on human sleep patterns for many years. Blue light is emitted by electronic devices such as smartphones, tablets, and computers, as well as by energy-efficient LED light bulbs. Research shows that exposure to blue light in the evening suppresses the production of melatonin, the hormone that regulates our sleep-wake cycle. This can lead to difficulty falling asleep, reduced quality of sleep, and daytime tiredness. A study conducted at Harvard Medical School found that people who used e-readers before bed took longer to fall asleep and were less alert the next morning compared to those who read printed books. Experts recommend avoiding screens for at least one hour before bedtime, using blue light filters on devices, or switching to warm-colored lighting in the evening. Some companies have also started producing special glasses that block blue light for people who must use screens at night.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (British Male)
paras: The history of the Olympic Games is divided into two main periods: the ancient Olympics and the modern Olympics. The ancient Olympic Games were held in Olympia, Greece, from 776 BC until they were abolished by the Roman Emperor Theodosius I in 393 AD, after more than 1,100 years of history. These ancient games were part of a religious festival honoring Zeus, the king of the Greek gods. Events included running, wrestling, chariot racing, and the pentathlon. The modern Olympic Games were revived by French educator Baron Pierre de Coubertin, who founded the International Olympic Committee in 1894. The first modern Olympics were held in Athens, Greece, in 1896, with just 14 countries and 241 athletes competing in 43 events. Today, the Summer and Winter Olympics alternate every two years, with thousands of athletes from more than 200 countries competing in hundreds of events. The Olympics have become the world's largest sporting event and a symbol of international cooperation and peace.
